papers.title: Object features survive motion at saccadic speed but lose their link to specific objects
papers.abstract: Saccadic eye movements sweep objects across the retina at high speed, and this motion is routinely omitted from conscious perception. Whether object identity survives such motion is unclear. In two preregistered experiments (N = 20 and N = 19), we asked how object motion at saccadic speeds, while the eyes fixate, affects object continuity in the object-reviewing paradigm (Kahneman et al., 1992; Sasi et al., 2023). Two Gabor patches each carried a digit, then disappeared and reappeared in place, reappeared displaced, or travelled continuously to their new locations; the intervening interval lasted 300 ms or was matched to the mean or peak speed of a saccade. A target digit then appeared in one patch, and participants identified it. At the long duration, we replicated the Object-Specific Preview Benefit (OSPB): responses were faster when the target had been previewed in that same object than in the other one. At saccadic durations, the OSPB disappeared, and adding a distinguishing surface feature in Experiment 2 did not restore it. The general preview benefit, faster responses to any previewed digit than to a new one, persisted at every duration. Object features therefore survive motion at saccadic speed, but their link to a particular object does not.

papers.title: Competing routes back to firing shape population hyperexcitability and its selective suppression
papers.abstract: Whether a neuron will fire again is fundamentally a different question from whether a quiescent neuron will activate. Even within the same neuron, successive spikes can follow distinct post-spike trajectories, with after-depolarization permitting early return to firing and depolarization block prolonging inactivity. Therefore, we propose that hyperexcitability involves changes in the opportunities to fire again across the spike cycle, and not just from quiescence. The firing hazard makes these opportunities measurable: in whole-cell recordings of midbrain dopamine neurons, the subthreshold voltage trough resolves a non-monotone aggregate firing hazard into physiologically distinguishable components. We represent these components as competing return pathways within a population renewal model and show that they lead to heterogeneous firing patterns within a single neuronal population subject to a common drive. An immediate-return pathway provides an early opportunity to fire by skipping some stages of recovery, and promotes population hyperexcitability independent of quiescent activation. Conversely, a sequestration pathway diverts recently active neurons into a prolonged non-recruitable state, representing depolarization block or use-dependent blockade. Pharmacological selectivity of anti-seizure medications such as phenytoin and carbamazepine arises from the redistribution of neurons among return pathways at every renewal, with fast-cycling pathological regimes providing more opportunities for renewal and eventual sequestration.

papers.title: Evidence-based re-identification: Leveraging appearance cues to correct tracking mistakes rather than trying to prevent them
papers.abstract: Naturalistic behavioral neuroscience experiments, in which groups of animals interact in enriched environments over prolonged periods, require each animal's identity to remain correct throughout the recording. Current multi-animal tracking tools assign identities frame by frame without revisiting past assignment decisions. A single, even sporadic, identity swap is therefore likely to persist until the end of the recording. Consequently, error-free tracking results become progressively less likely as recordings lengthen and cohorts grow. Even state-of-the-art multi-object tracking (MOT) methods that leverage appearance cues do so only to make each assignment more robust. This robustness, however, only delays the inevitable as even the most robust assignment process will eventually make a mistake over prolonged recordings. A mistake that will then persist just as it otherwise would have. Here, we introduce evidence-based re-identification, which uses appearance cues to correct tracking mistakes rather than prevent them. This fundamental shift allows the algorithm to build and progressively enrich appearance representations for each tracked subject. Tracking mistakes are then detected by continuously monitoring the evolution of these representations, triggering a correction whenever two representations drift toward one another in a sustained way. On two distinct, minutes-long benchmarks of mice interacting in enriched environments, motion-only trackers (DeepLabCut, SLEAP, ByteTrack) and the appearance-based BoT-SORT-ReID began accumulating identity errors within seconds, whereas ByteTrack paired with evidence-based re-identification remained reliable, outperforming even ByteTrack paired with the marker-based Tailtag system. This reliability was also positively correlated with the accuracy of the appearance extractor, but only when it was used through evidence-based re-identification. Foundation image encoders (CLIP, MegaDescriptor, DINOv3) showed promising out-of-the-box performance yet still required fine-tuning to be effective. Together, these results show that multi-animal tracking algorithms can remain reliable over prolonged periods only if they can reliably recover from tracking mistakes, and that fine-tuning appearance extractors remains essential to doing so.

papers.title: Spatial proteomics on repurposed sequencers reveals early astrocytic remodeling in an ALS mouse model
papers.abstract: Spatial proteomics can reveal how disease reshapes cells and their local environments, but extending these measurements across replicated tissue cohorts requires validated antibodies, consistent sample processing and integrated analysis. These requirements are particularly pressing in studies of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), where pathology evolves unevenly across spinal-cord regions and disease stages. Here, we established an end-to-end spatial proteomics workflow linking a validated 28-antibody panel to automated fluorescence decoding and imaging on repurposed high-throughput sequencers, followed by multicycle image processing, cellular profiling and probabilistic spatial-neighborhood analysis. We applied it to 70 lumbar spinal-cord sections from nine SOD1-G93A and nine wild-type mice at presymptomatic, disease-onset and symptomatic stages. Spatial neighborhood analysis revealed that the environments surrounding motor neurons were already remodeled at disease onset. GFAP-high neighborhoods expanded in the ventral gray matter, with 43% of motor neurons embedded in these environments in SOD1-G93A mice, compared with 15% in wild-type mice. This early expansion preceded the later decline of non-reactive gray matter and detectable motor-neuron loss. The regional organization of the protein-defined changes shared features with neuronal and astrocytic patterns mapped by spatial transcriptomics in mouse and human ALS. This work enables spatial proteomics across replicated tissue cohorts and identifies localized remodeling of the environments around surviving motor neurons as an early feature of disease in the SOD1-G93A model.

papers.title: Whole-Brain MRSI Metabolic Connectomics Reveals Network Disruptions and Altered Gradient Coherence in Psychosis Risk
papers.abstract: Brain network alterations preceding first-episode psychosis often escape connectomic approaches based on conventional neuroimaging, such as diffusion or functional magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Whole-brain magnetic resonance spectroscopic imaging (MRSI) offers a potentially more sensitive alternative: by mapping neurometabolites across the brain, it enables the construction of metabolic connectomes that may capture very early and subtle disruptions of brain network properties. We combined whole-brain proton MRSI, diffusion MRI, and resting-state functional MRI in a sample of 29 individuals meeting DSM-5 criteria for Attenuated Psychosis Syndrome (APS) or Schizotypal Personality Disorder (SCZT), pooled into a single High Risk for Psychosis (HR) group, and 30 healthy controls (HC) to construct metabolic, structural, and functional connectomes. Network-based statistics identified a significant metabolic connectivity subnetwork with higher connectivity in HR than in HC, whereas no corresponding structural or functional connectivity differences were detected. Nodes of this subnetwork had modestly higher structural strength but were not consistently enriched among structural hubs, and no significant regional abnormalities in individual metabolite concentrations were detected. Eigenmode analysis of metabolic connectivity revealed a low-dimensional organization spanning a posterior unimodal-to-transmodal axis and a transmodal-to-limbic axis. Path analysis revealed higher bilateral energy in HR, indicating reduced coherence along a metabolic gradient that parallels the neurodevelopmental sensorimotor-to-association axis. These findings identify whole-brain metabolic network organization derived from MRSI as a systems-level phenotype of psychosis risk and raise the possibility that it captures altered development of large-scale cortical organization.

papers.title: Sensory and Motor Building Blocks of an Extra Robotic Digit Representation
papers.abstract: Supernumerary limbs provide a unique opportunity to ask how the brain represents an entirely novel effector within an existing sensorimotor system. Here, we investigated how primary motor cortex (M1) represents a robotic extra digit (the Third Thumb; Dani Clode Design), and how this representation changes with experience. Using fMRI, we compared participants following short-term exposure with participants who had undergone longitudinal Third Thumb training. The device was controlled by the toes but operated alongside the biological fingers, while its sensory consequences were experienced on the hand. Following prolonged experience, greater activity was elicited in the M1 hand area both during Third Thumb control, and in response to its sensory consequences alone. Multivariate analyses showed that the Third Thumb representation became more distinct from its biological toe controller. Pattern component modelling further showed that the representation could be explained by a combination of its constituent motor and sensory patterns, but their relative contributions changed substantially with experience, from toe-dominated following short-term exposure to sensory-dominated following longitudinal training. These findings suggest that M1 can represent a novel effector through flexible recombination of existing sensorimotor representations, with experience altering how these pre-existing resources contribute to the emerging representation.

papers.title: Capturing continuous spectrotemporal pupil--brain coupling with simultaneous wearable EEG/Eye tracking
papers.abstract: Spontaneous fluctuations in pupil diameter are closely linked to neural dynamics, yet most evidence for pupil--brain coupling has been obtained in conventional laboratory settings. We therefore asked whether the spectrotemporal and directional organization of such coupling can be captured with wearable systems to test their use in naturalistic settings. Using combined lightweight mobile EEG (MUSE) and eye tracking (Tobii Pro Glasses 3) devices, we investigated resting-state pupil--brain coupling and explored interoceptive attention to determine whether the core organizational principles observed with stationary equipment are detectable within and preserved across continuous recording states. Cross-correlation, mutual information, and Granger causality analyses revealed that pupil--brain coupling displayed clear frequency-dependent organization. Lower EEG frequencies (2-12Hz) preceded pupil dynamics by roughly 764ms, while higher frequencies showed a distinct coupling range. Granger-causality analysis further indicated predominantly EEG-to-pupil directional coupling. Similar observations were made during interoception. Overall, these findings align well and extend previous evidence on spontaneous pupil--brain coupling, demonstrating that lightweight and movable wearable devices are suitable to characterize spectrotemporal and directional pupil--brain interactions. In turn, these results encourage future fundamental and translational research in naturalistic environments.

papers.title: Pharmaco-genetic evidence of presymptomatic lysosomal dysfunction coupled to detrimental DPR secretion in Drosophila Models of C9orf72-linked ALS/FTD.
papers.abstract: Hexanucleotide repeat expansions in C9orf72, the most common genetic cause of Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and frontotemporal dementia (FTD), drive neurodegeneration through both loss of gene function and toxic gain-of-function mechanisms, including transcription of repeat RNA and repeat-associated non-AUG (RAN) translation into dipeptide repeat proteins (DPRs). Both disease mechanisms have been linked to disruption of the autophagy-lysosome pathway (ALP), though how this contributes to disease progression remains unclear. By expressing toxic C9orf72 repeats in Drosophila melanogaster, we observed presymptomatic lysosome impairment, coupled with largely preserved autophagosome formation. Pharmacological treatment with valproic acid (VPA) partially prevented neurodegenerative and locomotor phenotypes in expressing animals in presence of Mitf, which is required for lysosomal biogenesis. Genetic inhibition of residual lysosomal degradation enhanced neurotoxicity, whereas downregulation of autophagy and secretory autophagy genes suppressed toxicity, uncovering a previously unrecognized contribution of secretion to disease. Consistent with this, in vitro experiments indicated that disabling lysosome function, but not autophagy induction, leads to an increase in neuronal release of autophagy-associated proteins and DPRs, which can be found be uptaken by nearby neurons and glia in vivo. We propose that repeat-driven presymptomatic lysosomal dysfunction, prevented by pharmacologic treatment, promotes secretory autophagy, which, in turn facilitates extracellular release and intercellular propagation of neurotoxic DPRs.

papers.title: HMGB1/CXCL12 heterocomplex activates CXCR4 to suppress the ability of Muller glia to become proliferating progenitor-like cells in the chick retina
papers.abstract: We investigated how High Mobility Group Box 1 (HMGB1) signaling regulates glial reactivity and Muller glia-derived progenitor cell (MGPC) formation in the chick retina. HMGB1 released from stressed cells is known to form a heterocomplex with C-X-C chemokine ligand 12 (CXCL12) to activate C-X-C chemokine receptor 4 (CXCR4). HMGB1 is broadly expressed in retinal neurons and glia and is rapidly exported from the nuclei of stressed inner retinal neurons after damage, a process blocked by inflachromene. Stressed or damaged amacrine cells also exported different transcription factors out nuclei. CXCL12 is expressed by amacrine, horizontal, and bipolar cells, whereas CXCR4 is expressed by Muller glia and is rapidly upregulated following damage. CXCR4 agonist or recombinant HMGB1/CXCL12 treatment selectively stimulates mTOR and Jak/Stat signaling in Muller glia in undamaged retinas. Inhibition of CXCR4 signaling, HMGB1 nuclear export, or HMGB1/CXCL12 complex formation potently stimulated MGPC proliferation without affecting neuronal death or microglial activation. In retinas treated with insulin and FGF2, to induce MGPC proliferation independent of injury, HMGB1 remains confined to nuclei, CXCR4 is downregulated, and inhibition of HMGB1 or CXCR4 has no effect. We further demonstrate that microglia are required to maintain CXCR4 expression in Muller glia, and blockade of HMGB1/CXCL12-CXCR4 signaling does not restore MGPC proliferation in microglia-depleted retinas. Together, these findings identify HMGB1/CXCL12-CXCR4 signaling as an injury-induced pathway that limits Muller glia reprogramming and MGPC formation in damaged retinas.

papers.title: A complete adult Drosophila melanogaster brain tracheolar network
papers.abstract: The tracheal system of the fruit fly, Drosophila melanogaster, is a complex network of epithelial tubules that supplies oxygen and removes carbon dioxide throughout the organism, with gases entering and exiting through spiracles along the body. While tracheal development and patterning in the embryonic and larval stages have been extensively studied, particularly in the body, much less is known about tracheal and tracheolar organization within the adult brain. To address this gap, we manually traced every tracheole in the brain of a female adult Drosophila using the Full Adult Fly Brain (FAFB) open-access electron microscopy dataset. We reconstructed 117 tracheoles that branch within the parenchyma, terminating in 1,376 endings without forming an interconnected network. Joint analysis of these skeleton reconstructions with volumetric mesh segmentations from the FlyWire connectome revealed that tracheole volume fraction is heterogeneous across neuropils and largely symmetric in overall tracheation between left and right hemispheres. We observe that synapses are not preferentially positioned near tracheoles, and are instead slightly depleted from a region approximately 15 um around tracheoles, relative to other points along the same neurons. We also quantify the relative proximity of neurotransmitter-specific synapses and cables to tracheoles across neuropils. This detailed anatomical description of the tracheolar network establishes a reference for future studies examining how neuronal patterning, activity, and metabolic demand couple with tracheole development and function.

papers.title: Mechanism and subunit-dependence of disease-associated lurcher mutation in AMPA-type glutamate receptors
papers.abstract: AMPA receptors are glutamate-activated neuroreceptors responsible for the majority of fast excitatory neurotransmission in vertebrate brains. Activity-dependent changes in their functional and trafficking properties underpin cognitive processes such as learning and memory formation. In the past 15 years, a number of mutations within AMPA receptor genes have been identified as disease-causing leading to some form of neurodevelopmental delay. Here, we focused on one such mutation called lurcher, resulting from a change of the third Ala in the highly conserved SYTANLAAF motif to Thr. We determined functional consequences of lurcher mutation in homomeric AMPA receptors composed of subunits GluA1 or GluA2. In GluA1 subunit, lurcher mutation has been identified as a hotspot in a large cohort of patients with neurodevelopmental disorders. We confirm previously established lurcher phenotype characterised by slower deactivation and desensitization kinetics as well as more profound block of desensitization compared to the wild-type (WT) homomers. We show that these effects are more pronounced in GluA2 than GluA1 homomers. Lurcher phenotypes are attenuated, but still present, in more physiologically abundant heteromeric AMPA receptors composed of two GluA1 lurcher and two GluA2 WT subunits (GluA1 lc/GluA2 WT). Schild analysis indicates lurcher enhances activity of AMPA receptors by primarily changing the efficiency with which they open their ion channel upon glutamate binding rather than by changing affinity for glutamate. Perampanel, the only widely licensed drug that targets AMPA receptors, is an anti-convulsant that acts as a non-competitive inhibitor. We show it continues to inhibit GluA1 lc/GluA2 WT heteromeric receptors and that its IC50 depends on the auxiliary subunits associated with the heteromers. Specifically, stargazin (TARP {gamma}-2) brings the IC50 for perampanel into the submicromolar range, just like in the WT receptors.

papers.title: Beyond organ age gaps: comparing plasma proteomic metrics of organ biology in relation to brain structure and neurodegenerative disease.
papers.abstract: Biological aging is heterogeneous across organ systems, and brain health may be influenced by biological processes extending beyond the central nervous system (CNS). This can be investigated using biological age measures that are increasingly used to estimate how biological systems deviate from chronological aging. However, organ level plasma proteomic metrics may capture different forms of biological variation depending on how they are defined. Here, we compared three complementary organ level proteomic metrics across 15 organ systems (and two global systems) in relation to age, organ-relevant physiological phenotypes, brain morphometry, and incident neurodegenerative disease, using plasma proteomics from 52,667 UK Biobank participants and brain MRI data from 5,078 of those individuals. We derived i) supervised age gap metrics using XGBoost models trained to predict chronological age, ii) unsupervised PC1 metrics capturing dominant organ-associated proteomic variation, and iii) phenotype guided PLS metrics linking plasma proteins to organ-relevant physiological traits. The three metric classes were related but not interchangeable. Global all-protein and all-organ-protein models showed strong age-related proteomic structure. However, organ-specific PC analyses showed that age was often but not always the dominant source of variation in protein signal across organs. Age gap metrics showed the most consistent associations with subsequent ICD-10-based neurodegenerative and vascular diagnoses, whereas all three metric classes showed distinct associations with brain structure and organ-relevant physiological phenotypes. Brain structure analyses revealed heterogeneous organ-brain association patterns across organs, suggesting that proteomic variation relates to brain structure in both a systemic and an organ-specific manner. Several systemic and organ-specific signals partially mediated the associations between disease specific genetic risk and incident diagnoses of Alzheimer's disease and stroke, albeit with small effect sizes (1-8%). Similarly, organ metrics provided modest incremental predictive improvement over baseline demographic models, with the largest increase in ROC-AUC observed for Alzheimer's disease when all organ age gap metrics were added jointly (delta ROC-AUC = 0.037). These results link brain related outcomes to proteomic variation across both CNS and non-CNS systems. Our work suggests that proteomic organ metrics capture complementary dimensions of biological variation rather than a single construct of organ aging. Although these measures may provide informative biological and potentially predictive signals, their incremental predictive value in the present analyses was modest.

papers.title: A trio of brain networks dynamically orchestrates music recognition
papers.abstract: Recognition memory continuously integrates internal representations with sensory information to guide adaptive behavior. Yet most theoretical models conceptualize recognition as the retrieval of an isolated stimulus through a discrete sequence of steps including sensory processing, hippocampal retrieval, and cortical reinstatement. However, in natural settings, perception, memory, and predictions interact continuously within an evolving context to guide adaptive responses. It is unclear how brain networks coordinate the integration of internal and external information during dynamic recognition. Here, we combined intracranial recordings (N = 30) of high-frequency activity (70-160 Hz) and dimensionality reduction to characterize distributed network dynamics during music recognition. We identified three interacting functional networks supporting sensory processing, sensory-memory integration, and decision formation, whose temporal dynamics predicted the timing of behavior. During recognition of memorized sequences, sensory activity progressively attenuated, sensory inputs were combined with mnemonic and contextual information, and decision-related activity evolved toward sensorimotor engagement. Novel sequences disrupted this organization by sustaining sensory responses and accelerating decision-related activity. Sensory and integrative networks communicated bidirectionally. Our findings reveal recognition as a distributed, context-dependent, and goal-directed process emerging from the continuous and bidirectional coordination of large-scale brain networks.

papers.title: Neural Encoding Geometry of Human Voluntary Visual Selection
papers.abstract: Selecting relevant targets from competing alternatives is a core cognitive function. While human visual selection can be tracked with high spatiotemporal precision, it remains unsolved how selected targets and non-selected alternatives are neurally encoded to effectively separate them. Building on recent work revealing the neural encoding geometry underlying target selection in animals, we here examined how the representational format of selected targets and non-selected alternatives evolve over time during human voluntary selection. Initially, selected and non-selected objects showed equal spatially selective neural activity, yet the selected target was represented more strongly after 300-350 ms. Using cross-decoding, we found that selected and non-selected objects are encoded along a shared sensory axis, whereas selected targets are encoded along an additional spatially selective axis. This encoding geometry effectively separates selected targets from non-selected alternatives in neural space. Our results generalized across selection conditions: we found comparable results in instructed and free-choice selection, as well as in delayed oculomotor and covert visual selection. Together, we demonstrate that the human brain selectively encodes targets, but not distractors, along an additional axis, revealing a neural mechanism through which voluntary selection prioritizes behaviorally relevant information.

papers.title: Geometry-Conditioned Hyperalignment for Generalizable EEG Decoding Across Datasets and Paradigms
papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) supports promising applications, but daily use remains limited by poor cross-subject and cross-dataset generalisation. That is because EEG recordings made with different electrode montages do not even share an observation space, and each subjects's leadfield projects the same neural sources onto the scalp differently. We present hTSMNet, which combines a novel geometry-conditioned hyperalignment frontend with a Riemannian symmetric positive-definite (SPD) manifold backbone that reduces the residual cross-subject distribution shift. From electrode coordinates alone, the frontend builds a linear map from any montage onto a fixed set of scalp anchors, placing every recording in one shared space. Because this map has no subjectspecific parameters, an unseen subject, dataset, or montage is aligned from its geometry alone, so transfer is zero-shot by construction. On a leave-one-dataset-out left-/right-hand motor-imagery (MI) benchmark across three datasets (172 subjects) and eight comparators, hTSMNet matches the strongest comparator at strict zero-shot, and attains the highest accuracy on every dataset once a few calibration trials for adjusting only final-layer classifier are available. We show that it orients the binary decision the same way in every dataset, so that a single linear rule learned on the source data is already correctly oriented on a held-out one. The same frozen MI-pretrained model also transfers across paradigms: with only a re-fit final-layer classifier, hTSMNet decodes mental workload and steady-state visual evoked potentials (SSVEP) well above chance, yet remains at chance on stimulus-locked event-related potentials (ERP). This dissociation follows from the architecture: covariance pooling reads oscillatory band power and is largely insensitive to the phase-locked potentials that ERP tasks depend on. What the representation generalizes is a signal family (band-limited oscillatory activity), not the named task. Geometry-conditioned hyperalignment thus yields an inspectable representation, which is generalizable across datasets and, within the oscillatory regime, across paradigms.

papers.title: Early visual experience redistributes cFos-tagged neurons toward the cortex while preserving presynaptic spatial stereotypy
papers.abstract: The macroscale functional organization of the brain is spatially stereotyped across individuals, but whether this extends to finer spatial scales is not known. Furthermore, how experience shapes this organization across the brain remains unclear. To address this, we developed cFos promoter-driven reporter mouse lines that permanently label either the cell bodies or presynaptic terminals of neurons during defined temporal windows. Using serial two-photon tomography and voxel-wise statistics, we mapped brain-wide distributions of cFos-tagged somata or their presynaptic terminals during the first week of visual experience or its deprivation. We found that midbrain and subcortical regions show greater stereotypy for cFos-tagged neurons and their presynaptic terminals compared to cortical regions. This fine-scale spatial stereotypy remained largely preserved despite visual deprivation, which shifted the relative recruitment of cFos-tagged neurons from cortical toward the highly stereotyped midbrain and subcortical regions. Our findings identify heterogeneous, spatially constrained functional organization across the brain that is conserved across subjects yet accommodates experience-dependent reorganization of neuronal recruitment.

papers.title: Beyond Exploration: Heightened Recent Reward Reliance and Midfrontal Sensitivity to Outcome Differences in ADHD
papers.abstract: Adaptive decision-making requires balancing the exploitation of known rewards with the exploration of alternative options, yet how attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) shapes this trade-off remains unclear. Using a restless four-armed bandit task and electroencephalography (EEG), we investigated the neural correlates of exploratory decisions and how recent rewards shape choice behavior and feedback processing in 23 adults with self-reported clinical ADHD diagnoses and 27 controls. Across 450 trials with dynamically changing payoffs, choices were classified against the highest last-observed payoff, and behavioral modeling quantified the influence of reward history on subsequent decisions. Contrary to our predictions, exploration rates, task performance, and neural differentiation between exploration and exploitation did not differ significantly between groups. However, adults with ADHD were more likely to repeat an option after high reward feedback and switch after low rewards, driven primarily by the immediately preceding outcome. At neural level, ADHD participants also showed greater midfrontal sensitivity to unsigned changes between consecutive payoffs, expressed in a feedback-evoked response spanning 280 to 568 ms and carried by slow activity below 2 Hz. Together, these findings dissociate the raw frequency of exploration from the dynamic weighting of recent outcomes in ADHD. Rather than reflecting an indiscriminate drive for novelty, behavior was characterized by heightened recent reward reliance paired with amplified slow-wave midfrontal sensitivity to outcome shifts. Crucially, this profile emerged without compromising overall performance, suggesting that, in this volatile environment, ADHD was associated with an increased weighting of recent outcomes rather than with a performance deficit.

papers.title: Computational model of developmental self-assembly of a cortical microcircuit
papers.abstract: Cortical microcircuits emerge from local developmental interactions, yet large-scale computational models typically prescribe connectivity rather than explain its formation. Here we use BioDynaMo to simulate the self-assembly of ~70,000 cortical neurons from 1,200 progenitors in 3D physical space through migration, neurite growth and contact-based synapse formation. With one calibrated filling fraction per connection type, the locally formed synapses reproduce experimentally measured connectivity across 64 connection types (mean absolute error 0.0062) without prescribing individual connections. The grown spiking networks sustain stable, inhibition-dominated activity, and the same developmental rules, given different targets, generate both a canonical cortical microcircuit and a visual-cortex variant. Inverting the migration programme produces a reeler-like column whose aberrant connectivity destabilises network activity. Together, these findings provide a mechanistic link between local developmental processes and the emergence of cortical anatomy, connectivity and function.

papers.title: Somatic symptom burden is associated with anger internalization measured as reduced reactive aggression
papers.abstract: Difficulties in emotion regulation, including anger suppression, have been linked to more severe somatic symptoms in patients with chronic pain. Because this evidence comes mainly from clinical samples, it remains unclear whether such difficulties precede or follow symptom chronification. We examined whether somatic symptom burden is associated with reduced reactive aggression, as a behavioral marker of anger internalization. Forty-four healthy adults (25 females) completed the Taylor Aggression Paradigm, a competitive reaction-time task in which they selected noise intensity delivered to a fictitious opponent across three provocation conditions (low, moderate, and high). somatic symptom burden was evaluated using the Somatic Symptom Scale-8 (SSS-8) and Patient Health Questionnaire-15 (PHQ-15). Alexithymia was evaluated using the Toronto Alexithymia Scale (TAS-20). Participants with higher somatic symptom burden selected lower noise intensities overall, with significant differences at low and moderate provocation levels. Difficulty identifying feelings tended to be positively associated with somatic symptom burden, whereas alexithymia was not associated with reactive aggression. These findings suggest that inhibited retaliation, previously reported in chronic pain patients, may already be present in healthy individuals with higher somatic symptom burden, potentially aiding early identification of chronic pain risk. Difficulty distinguishing emotions from bodily sensations may also contribute to somatic symptom expression.

papers.title: PhyMorphS: A Physics-Guided Framework for Mesh-Based Morphological Synthesis of White Matter Microstructures
papers.abstract: Numerical phantoms provide controlled 3D representations of brain tissue microstructure for developing and evaluating biophysical models of diffusion-weighted Magnetic Resonance Imaging (dMRI). Existing phantom synthesizers employ different geometric primitives and optimization strategies to generate densely packed substrates with diverse axonal morphologies. However, direct deformation of axonal surfaces under mechanical constraints remains less explored. We propose PhyMorphS, a mesh-based framework in which axonal morphology emerges through physics-guided growth and interactions with the local microstructural environment, without constraining cross-sections to predefined symmetric shapes. In PhyMorphS, axons, myelin sheaths, and cell bodies are represented by triangle meshes, while a mass-spring system and collision-resolution scheme guide iterative axonal growth under mechanical and packing constraints. This enables irregular, asymmetric, and non-convex cross-sections, longitudinal diameter variation, and user-defined morphological alterations such as axonal beading and myelin layer decompaction. We evaluate PhyMorphS against large-scale X-ray nano-holotomography segmentations of real 3D axons from four white matter regions with distinct fiber organizations. The synthesized axons reproduce key region-specific morphological characteristics and achieve high packing densities, while the parallelized implementation scales approximately linearly with axon count in the generation voxel. By reproducing the geometric variability observed in real WM tissue, PhyMorphS provides controlled substrates for investigating how realistic morphology influences simulated dMRI signals, testing the geometric assumptions of biophysical microstructure models, and generating diverse paired microstructure-signal datasets for training machine-learning models.

papers.title: Multiplexed mapping of long-range projections with FluoCode, a combinatorial fluorescent barcoding system
papers.abstract: Comprehensive mapping of long-range projections remains a major challenge in neuroscience. Conventional virus tracing labels only one or a few pathways per animal, and inter-individual comparison requires registering whole-brain images to a standard atlas. However, inter-individual variability in morphology and wiring limits fine-scale mapping. Here we report "FluoCode", a combinatorial fluorescent barcoding system for multiplexed projection mapping within single animals. We developed adeno-associated virus (AAV) vectors that express two of seven different fluorescent proteins, yielding 21 distinct color codes, and a "FluoCode Reader" that automatically classifies neurite signals by color combinations and morphology. Using FluoCode, we mapped projections from up to 21 cortical areas to subcortical regions in individual mice, revealing fine-scale topographic maps in small subcortical nuclei. In the marmoset, mapping from the primary visual cortex demonstrated topographic projections in higher visual areas and thalamic nuclei. FluoCode thus enables fine-scale, within-animal comparison of long-range projections in rodents and primates.

papers.title: Pupil size reflects effort but not motor fatigability during a sustained motor task
papers.abstract: Pupil size has been shown to reflect physical effort during brief, discrete motor tasks. It remains unknown whether pupil size similarly scales with effort during sustained repetitive movement, or whether it also reflects the accumulation of motor fatigability, a reduction in motor performance during prolonged movements. In our previous work, sustained maximal tapping induced motor slowing, a subtype of motor fatigability, characterized by decreasing movement speed and associated with increased antagonistic muscle coactivation. Next to these behavioural effects, pupil initially dilated and then gradually decreased over time. Whether this temporal change in pupil size is shaped by physical effort alone or also by motor fatigability remains unclear. Here, we combined a repetitive wrist tapping paradigm with force measurement, electromyography, and pupillometry, and paced participants at three different tapping speeds to dissociate physical effort from motor slowing, which has been shown to be speed-dependent. Fatigability-related motor slowing emerged selectively at the fastest speed. Moreover, we showed that antagonistic muscle coactivation increased more steeply at faster speeds, even in the absence of motor slowing, suggesting it may reflect an early change in motor control. While we found clear evidence that pupil size scaled with overall tapping speed, we did not find evidence that the temporal change of the pupil was pacing-dependent. These findings extend the pupil effort relationship to sustained, dynamic motor tasks and suggest that pupil size is a marker of physical effort but not motor fatigability during sustained repetitive movement.

papers.title: Maternal deprivation impairs social recognition by diminishing the number of adult-born granule cells in the dentate gyrus
papers.abstract: Childhood neglect increases the likelihood of developing neuropsychiatric disease in adulthood. Maternal separation and early weaning (MSEW), a rodent model of maternal deprivation, was used to investigate effects on social recognition, a commonly impaired function in neuropsychiatric disorders in humans. We found that in adulthood, MSEW male mice showed social recognition impairments, and that MSEW female mice showed greater preference fo social novelty. MSEW male, but not female, mice had diminished numbers of adult-born granule cells (abGCs) in the dentate gyrus, as well as a lower density of abGC axons in the CA2 region compared to controls. MSEW males also showed a reduced rate of sharp wave ripples (SWRs) in the CA2 region in response to novel mouse exposure, as well as a reduction in differential SWR rates in response to novel and familiar mouse exposure. Living in an enriched environment restored the number of abGCs in the dentate gyrus of MSEW males to control levels and improved social recognition. Furthermore, chemogenetic activation of 4-6 week old, but not older, abGCs in a double transgenic model improved social recognition and partially restored CA2 SWR patterns in MSEW mice. These findings suggest that MSEW impairs social recognition through diminished adult neurogenesis, which can be restored in adulthood by living in a proneurogenic environment or by increasing the activity of existing abGCs.

papers.title: NeuroDisco: Interfacing neuronal populations - cell by cell, millisecond by millisecond, day by day
papers.abstract: Neuronal cultures offer comprehensive access to living networks, but their value as functional models is limited by synchronized bursts that drive pathologically strong neuronal depolarization. Theory attributes such bursting to a lack of external input. Here we present NeuroDiscos, compact {micro}LED and OLED projectors that operate inside standard incubators and deliver patterned, long-term optogenetic stimulation, synchronized with submillisecond precision to multi-electrode array recordings. Weak, uncorrelated NeuroDisco stimulation dispersed the bursts but left the population firing rate largely unchanged. In this asynchronous regime, neuronal activity reproducibly follows the weak stimulation, and stimulus-response relations characterize receptive fields and putative functional connections. At hardware costs of {euro}500-1,000, NeuroDiscos offer a scalable route to functional characterization of primary and patient-derived cultures.

papers.title: Brain Network Dynamics from Neuronal Avalanches for Longitudinal Motor-Imagery Decoding
papers.abstract: Brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) offer opportunities for personalized neurorehabilitation, but inter-session variability, repeated calibration, and the need for expert supervision limit their use beyond supervised settings. We propose a longitudinal BCI framework that integrates neuronal avalanches dynamics, reflecting cascades of propagation neural activity, with graph-theory and data-driven region of interest analysis to extract computationally efficient and neuro-physiological interpretable features. Source-reconstructed EEG from 20 BCI-naive participants performing right-hand motor imagery (MI) and rest across four training sessions was represented by a directed weighted connectivity network based on neuronal avalanches. Local, mesoscopic, and global network measures revealed task-related changes predominantly in contralateral sensorimotor regions and distributed reorganisation across training. We modelled here the learning-related evolution of feature distributions across previous sessions and used this trajectory to predict class-conditional distributions in an unseen fourth session, anticipating future brain states before new session calibration. PageRank-based ROI selection achieved an AUC of 73.5 +/- 7.9%, compared with 64.5 +/- 10.6% using all ROIs, while reducing computational time by approximately 39% relative to performance-driven selection. The proposed framework provides interpretable, compact descriptions of avalanche propagation and exploits training-related changes for prospective decoding. Moving spatial selection and model optimization to an initial offline phase may reduce subsequent calibration demands and facilitate more autonomous BCI use.

papers.title: Working memory capacity is linked to directed exploration: behavioral, computational, and electrophysiological evidence
papers.abstract: Balancing the exploitation of known rewards against the exploration of uncertain options is central to adaptive decision making, yet the cognitive limits on strategic exploration are poorly understood. Directed exploration, the deliberate sampling of uncertain options for information, may depend on working memory (WM), but whether WM capacity (WMC) is selectively related to it, and through which processes, is unknown. 52 participants from the upper and lower tails of an operation-span distribution (26 high-WMC, 26 low-WMC) performed an adapted Horizon Task during EEG recording. We combined behavioral strategy classification, hierarchical Bayesian reinforcement learning, stimulus-locked event-related potentials (ERPs), and an exploratory Bayesian mediation analysis. High-WMC participants showed more directed exploration and less exploitation, with no group difference in random exploration. A model in which accumulated sampling history discounts option value best explained choices in both groups, and the discounting parameter {omega} was larger in the high-WMC group. Statistically, {omega} accounted for the association between WMC and directed exploration (indirect effect ab = 0.64, 95% CrI [0.28, 1.05]). Frontocentral P2 amplitude (180 to 280 ms) during directed exploration was larger in the high-WMC group, and the P2 difference between directed exploration and exploitation correlated with behavioral preference for directed exploration (r = .29, p = .040). These findings suggest that individual differences in exploration may reflect not only the willingness to seek information but also the capacity to use what has been sampled. The WMC-related difference lay in information use rather than choice noise and was already visible in early option evaluation.

papers.title: Open-BEATBox: an open-source autonomous operant chamber for high-throughput data acquisition of complex behaviour
papers.abstract: Behavioural neuroscience increasingly relies on rodent models to investigate the neural mechanisms underlying cognition in health and disease. However, conventional operant testing is typically restricted to short daily sessions that require frequent experimenter intervention and often rely on food or water restriction. These constraints limit behavioural sampling, disrupt natural activity patterns, and introduce variability associated with handling and experimental schedules.Here, we present the Open Platform for Experimental Neuroscience Behavioural and Autonomous Box (Open-BEATBox), an open-source, autonomous home-cage platform that enables continuous, self-paced assessment of complex cognitive behaviour in mice. By allowing animals to live in the testing environment throughout the experiment, Open-BEATBox supports longitudinal behavioural assessment across different cognitive tasks while minimizing experimenter intervention and preserving natural circadian activity. The platform is modular, customizable, and designed to accommodate a broad range of operant paradigms and integration with chronic neural recording and neuromodulation technologies.Using a visual reversal-learning task, we show that continuous autonomous testing generates approximately ten times more completed trials during reversal learning than conventional session-based protocols while reducing experimenter workload without evidence of major adverse effects on the welfare measures assessed. The flexibility of the platform further enables implementation of additional cognitive paradigms, including uncertainty-based decision-making tasks.Together, Open-BEATBox provides an accessible open platform for longitudinal cognitive phenotyping, facilitating the collection of large longitudinal behavioural datasets and creating new opportunities to combine continuous behavioural assessment with modern systems neuroscience approaches.

papers.title: The neural circuit implementation of distributional reinforcement learning
papers.abstract: Distributional reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms outperform traditional RL by representing the full probability distribution of future outcomes rather than its mean. Neural signatures consistent with distributional coding have been observed in dopamine neurons and in striatal value representations. However, how distributional RL is implemented within the anatomical circuit organization of the basal ganglia remains unknown. Uncovering how representations of outcome distributions are organized across brain circuits has broad implications for both fundamental and clinical neuroscience, providing new insights into how the brain represents uncertainty and how these representations shape risk-sensitive learning and decision-making. Here, we investigated how representations of outcome distributions are organized across dopamine projections to the striatum by combining striatum-wide fiber photometry of dopamine axonal activity with Neuropixels recordings from projection-defined dopamine neurons. We found that distributional reward prediction error signals are preferentially encoded in lateral ventral striatum-projecting dopamine neurons, but that reward distribution information is shared between the ventral and the dorsal striatum. Additionally, an anatomical gradient of optimism in the midbrain supports the diversity of value predictions required for distributional RL. Our findings extend the actor-critic framework proposed for the basal ganglia by revealing distributional prediction errors in a subpopulation of mesolimbic dopamine neurons capable of training parallel striatal regions thought to implement different types of behavioral control.

papers.title: Tendon-specific PIEZO1 activation enhances neural drive to muscle during ballistic movement
papers.abstract: Tendons are generally regarded as passive structures that transmit muscle force to bone, yet they contain the Golgi tendon organ (GTO), whose Ib afferents act on motor neurons either inhibitory or excitatory depending on movement context. Whether a change in tendon mechanical properties alters the neural drive to muscle during movement remains unknown. We therefore recorded electromyography (EMG) and ankle kinematics during jumping in male mice carrying a tendon-specific gain-of-function (GOF) mutation in the mechanosensitive channel PIEZO1, which renders the tendon more compliant. In wild-type (WT) mice, gastrocnemius EMG amplitude increased with jump distance but not tibialis anterior activity, identifying the gastrocnemius as the muscle that scales with jump demand. At their maximum jump distance, which was longer in GOF than in WT mice, GOF mice showed a larger gastrocnemius EMG amplitude with unchanged burst duration. No genotype difference was detected at a submaximal distance, indicating that this enhancement depends on load. Kinematics showed the same specificity: GOF mice reached a deeper peak dorsiflexion before takeoff only at maximum jump distance, and the EMG difference emerged only after maximal dorsiflexion, not at burst onset. Muscle mass and myogenic gene expression were unchanged, whereas tendon marker genes were elevated, indicating that the enhancement was not of muscular origin. These findings indicate that a change in tendon mechanical properties alters the neural drive to muscle in a load-dependent manner, most plausibly through positive force feedback from the GTO, and identify the tendon as a sensory organ whose mechanical properties shape motor output.

papers.title: Subcellular Spatial Profiling Unveils Links Between Neuritic Plaques with Selective Tau Vulnerability in Alzheimer's Disease
papers.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) features widespread extracellular amyloid-{beta} plaques but selective intraneuronal tau accumulation in cortical layers II/III and V, while layer IV remains relatively resistant. Here, we combined subcellular spatial transcriptomics with co-registered A{beta} and pTau immunohistochemistry to determine why neurons exposed to comparable plaque-associated pathology differ in somatic pTau accumulation. Plaque-associated neuritic stress occurred similarly across layers, but layer IV neurons showed attenuated pTau accumulation and reduced somatic expression of a shared neurite-soma stress program involving DCTN1, CALM3, NORAD, and PIN1. Trajectory analysis within layers identified tau-vulnerable and resistant neuronal states implicating calcium signaling, retrograde transport, and lysosomal function. Notably, astrocytic APOE-neuronal LRP1 co-expression increased significantly along the pTau-vulnerable trajectory, and APOE {epsilon}4 was associated with stronger coupling of local plaque pathology to pTau-associated molecular programs. These findings reveal neuronal programs and neuron-glia interactions underlying selective tau vulnerability and resistance in AD, highlighting potential tau-targeting therapeutics.
